doc.title: Michael Abene interviewed by Monk Rowe, Toronto, Canada, January 11, 2003

title: Working with Joe Williams
summary: He tells how a synth-sounds chart led to writing for Joe Williams, and calls Williams a kind man.

story.theme_name: Singers and the musicians who accompanied them
story.community_name: Joe Williams: the singer with Basie

blocks.x: Tell me about working with Joe Williams.

I just did a couple of things with him. In fact it was at this club Buddy Rich had in New York called Buddy’s Place. And I did a couple of things with Joe. I would have liked to have done more, we just couldn’t connect with schedules. It was just impossible. But we did — one of the records I produced for GRP was a thing called “Happy Anniversary Charlie Brown.”
So Joe did something, was it “A Little Birdie?” I can’t remember.

So the day we were going to do it Joe was sick so he wasn’t there in the studio. So it was Greg Phillinganes, who is a wonderful synth keyboard player. I forget who else, Al Aarons from Basie’s band playing trumpet. I was playing another keyboard. I forget who the rest of the rhythm section was. And I wrote a chart, like horns, saxophone sounds and everything. So Joe comes in like a week later and boy he sounds great. So I get a call from John Levy, his manager, he says, “Joe wanted to see if he could use that chart, he’s doing ‘The Tonight Show.’” I said, “well I’ve got to tell you, that was all synth sounds, all the saxes.” He says, “wow,” he says, “could you write a chart for Joe?” I says, “well
yeah it’s easy, the chart’s there, I mean the chart’s all written on scratch paper, we just used —” So I went and wrote this chart. It sounded exactly the same.

But it was funny. And it did sound really terrific. You’d play that and you would have no idea it was like emulated saxophone sounds or brass sounds. Except for the live trumpet and live rhythm. But Joe said, “man, that was killing.” So John said, “well can you do the chart?” “Yeah the chart’s all there, you just have to write it out for the live horns, man, and you’ve got it.
So that was good. But I loved — Bobby Cranshaw got me involved with Joe in a couple of things. But he was fun to play behind. But Norman Simmons owned that gig. He owned that gig.
Sure. Well Joe helped us actually get this whole project started actually.
Oh I didn’t know that. He was a great guy.
He was a very good friend of ours.
He was just a kind man, I felt, really kind.
